strengths: Insightful problem formulation: The paper clearly articulates a key discrepancy between standard ReID training (aiming for general global discrimination across identities) and multi-object tracking (demanding sequence-specific, fine-grained discrimination among a small set of concurrent targets).

Principled and training-free method: Adapting Fisher Linear Discriminant (FLD) to dynamically find sequence- and time-adapted subspaces using trajectory histories provides an elegant, closed-form, and interpretable solution without requiring additional training or complex heuristic pipelines.

Strong empirical gains on appearance-only tracking: On appearance-challenging benchmarks like DanceTrack and SportsMOT, the proposed HAT-FastReID-MOT yields massive improvements over the appearance baseline (+10.6 HOTA on DanceTrack, +12.0 HOTA on SportsMOT), achieving performance competitive with or superior to advanced motion- and hybrid-based methods.

Comprehensive validation and ablations: The ablations thoroughly examine the impact of FLD vs. PCA, queue length T, temporal shift weighting, and knowledge integration, complemented by zero-shot transfer experiments across several vision backbones.
Clarity and presentation: The manuscript is well-structured, clearly written, and accompanied by helpful qualitative visualizations (Figures 1, 3, and 4).
weaknesses: Mathematical clarity regarding FLD singularity / Small Sample Size (SSS) problem: With standard feature dimensions (e.g., D = 2048 in FastReID) and typical MOT queue sizes (e.g., T = 60 across C ≈ 5–20 active targets, yielding N < D), the within-class scatter matrix S_W is mathematically singular and non-invertible. The manuscript does not specify how S_W^{-1} is regularized or computed (e.g., pseudo-inverse, diagonal regularization / Ledoit-Wolf shrinkage, or two-stage PCA-FLD). Clarifying this is essential for reproducibility and technical completeness.

Bootstrapping and handling of short / newborn trajectories: At the beginning of a sequence or when new targets appear, the history queues are either empty or contain very few frames, making covariance estimation unreliable. The paper does not clearly explain how the projection matrix is stabilized or bypassed during these early frames.

Computational overhead and deployment constraints: Computing the generalized eigenvalue decomposition at every frame incurs noticeable computational cost (as discussed in Appendix B.1, 22.7 FPS on GPU/CPU excluding detection). Because generalized eigensolvers are primarily executed on CPU in common scientific libraries, scaling to crowded scenes with high target counts or running on edge devices could be challenging.

Missing integration into modern hybrid trackers: While the authors deliberately isolate an appearance-only baseline to prevent confounding factors—which is methodologically sound—demonstrating whether HAT translates into additive gains when plugged into standard hybrid trackers (e.g., BoT-SORT, Deep OC-SORT) would significantly strengthen its practical value to the MOT community.

strengths: Insightful problem formulation: The paper clearly articulates the fundamental discrepancy between generic ReID (which optimizes for open-world separation across diverse identities) and sequence-level MOT (which requires fine-grained separation among a small, specific set of often highly similar targets).

Principled, training-free solution: Reformulating trajectory assignment features via Fisher Linear Discriminant (FLD) provides an elegant, closed-form, training-free way to adapt feature representations online to the active sequence context.

Rigorous and transparent experimental setup: Evaluating the proposed module on a pure ReID-based baseline isolates the contribution of appearance transformation cleanly, avoiding the confounding heuristics and cascades common in complex hybrid trackers.

Strong empirical gains: The approach achieves substantial performance improvements on benchmarks where targets share very similar appearances (e.g., DanceTrack and SportsMOT), demonstrating marked improvements in Association Accuracy (AssA) and IDF1 across multiple visual backbones.
weaknesses: Lack of discussion on numerical stability and singularity of the within-class scatter matrix: When the feature dimension is large ($D = 2048$) and historical samples are limited ($N \ll D$ or early in the video), the within-class scatter matrix $S_W$ is prone to singularity or ill-conditioning. The paper does not specify how this classic small-sample-size problem in FLD is handled (e.g., via shrinkage, ridge regularization $\epsilon I$, or pseudo-inversion).

Missing evaluation on standard hybrid/motion-based trackers: While testing on a pure ReID baseline provides clean ablation, in practical MOT systems, appearance is combined with Kalman filtering or learned motion models. Demonstrating that HAT consistently boosts competitive hybrid trackers (e.g., Deep OC-SORT, BoT-SORT) would substantially reinforce its real-world utility.

Runtime and scalability considerations: Computing the generalized eigenvalue problem on CPU per frame introduces latency (reported at ~22.7 FPS on a high-end setup with detection precomputed). For extremely crowded scenes with high track counts and continuous identity creation, the scalability and overhead could become a limiting factor.

strengths: Sound conceptual insight: The paper clearly identifies a fundamental misalignment between the goal of general ReID (global identity separation across vast populations) and MOT (local, fine-grained discrimination among a bounded set of co-occurring tracks in a sequence).

Principled and lightweight formulation: Formulating sequence-specific feature adaptation via Fisher Linear Discriminant (FLD) is training-free and provides an analytical, closed-form solution. The specific adaptations—temporally decayed trajectory centroids and blending with the original representation space (knowledge integration)—are technically sound and well-tailored for tracking dynamics.

Impressive empirical improvements on feature-based tracking: The proposed HAT consistently brings substantial performance gains to a purely ReID-based tracker across multiple challenging benchmarks, notably improving HOTA by +10.6 on DanceTrack and +13.5 on SportsMOT over the baseline, matching or surpassing sophisticated motion/hybrid tracking frameworks.

Thorough ablations and cross-paradigm evaluation: The experimental validation is extensive, comparing FLD against PCA, examining historical queue lengths, decay factors, and fusion weights, as well as showing consistent gains across multiple zero-shot visual encoders (MASA).
weaknesses: Handling of singularity and the cold-start phase: In high-dimensional feature spaces (e.g., $D=2048$) with few samples per track in early video frames, the within-class scatter matrix $S_W$ is inherently rank-deficient and singular. The paper does not adequately detail whether/how matrix regularization or pseudo-inverses are implemented to ensure numerical stability during these initial steps.

Computational overhead of online eigenvalue decomposition: Solving the generalized eigenvalue problem per frame incurs a noticeable computational cost (running at 22.7 FPS on DanceTrack detections using CPU scipy solvers). Scaling to crowded scenes with high track counts or higher-dimensional embeddings could become a throughput bottleneck.

Integration with modern motion-based frameworks: While evaluating on a pure ReID baseline effectively isolates the contribution of the feature transformation, it leaves open the practical question of whether HAT provides complementary benefits when incorporated into top-tier hybrid trackers (e.g., Deep OC-SORT or DiffMOT) that leverage both motion and appearance.

Minor mathematical typo and figure inconsistency: In Eq. (6), the class centroid calculation is written as $m_c = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{x \in X_c} x$ instead of dividing by the class size $N_c$. In Figure 4, panels are labeled as both 'LDA Transformed Features' and 'FLD Transformed Features' without clarifying the distinction between the two.

strengths: Insightful and sound motivation: The paper clearly identifies a fundamental conceptual mismatch in the tracking-by-detection literature—namely, treating MOT identity matching as an open-set retrieval problem using off-the-shelf ReID embeddings, rather than a sequence-specific closed-set discrimination problem. The correlation analysis between discriminability margin (\delta_{1000}) and association accuracy provides solid empirical grounding.

Simple, elegant, and training-free formulation: Leveraging Fisher Linear Discriminant (FLD) dynamically online using historical tracklets as pseudo-classes is a neat and mathematically principled approach. The task-specific adaptations—temporal weighting of track centroids and similarity-level knowledge integration—are well-motivated and directly address real-world tracking dynamics and newborn targets.

Comprehensive and rigorous experiments: The evaluation covers pure appearance trackers, multiple hybrid trackers (ByteTrack, OC-SORT, Hybrid-SORT), foundation-model feature extractors via MASA (ResNet-50, Detic, Grounding DINO, SAM), and diverse benchmarks (DanceTrack, SportsMOT, TAO, MOT17, MOT20).

Substantial gains on visually ambiguous benchmarks: The method yields dramatic gains on challenging datasets characterized by uniform appearance and complex motion (e.g., DanceTrack AssA improves from 31.6 to 46.0 on the pure ReID baseline, and boosts hybrid trackers significantly on SportsMOT and DanceTrack).

Transparent and thorough ablations: The comparisons between PCA and FLD, supervised offline FLD vs. online history-aware FLD, and the honest discussion of computational bottlenecks (generalized eigenvalue solver on CPU) and limitations on distinct-appearance datasets (MOT17) reflect strong scientific integrity.
weaknesses: Vulnerability to error propagation: Because FLD uses online historical tracklet assignments as pseudo-labels, early identity switches or tracking drift could corrupt the within-class and between-class scatter matrices, potentially reinforcing association errors over time. A more explicit analysis of recovery from early tracking failures would strengthen the paper.

Limited impact on appearance-distinct benchmarks: As acknowledged by the authors, the gains on MOT17, MOT20, and TAO are comparatively modest (e.g., MOT17 hybrid tracking gains are marginal, +0.1 HOTA), indicating that the technique primarily benefits scenarios where appearance is uniform and confusing.

Computational overhead of online generalized eigenvalue decomposition: Solving the generalized eigenvalue problem (S_B w = \lambda S_W w) per frame at high feature dimensions (d = 2048) cuts the association frame rate in half (from 46.5 to 22.7 FPS on DanceTrack), which poses practical constraints for resource-limited or real-time embedded deployment.

Heuristic selection and tuning of hyperparameters: The pipeline introduces several hyperparameters (history length T, decay coefficient \lambda_0, and balancing weight \alpha). While sensitivity analyses are provided, optimal performance across different visual backbones and datasets required dataset-specific tuning (e.g., adjusting \alpha for MASA and tuning hyperparameters for '†' results).

strengths: Compelling and intuitive motivation: The paper clearly identifies a fundamental conceptual mismatch between the generic, open-set objective of pre-trained ReID backbones and the sequence-specific, closed-set nature of association in Multiple Object Tracking (MOT).

Principled and training-free method: Formulating the context adaptation as an online Fisher Linear Discriminant (FLD) projection is mathematically sound, elegant, and requires no auxiliary training or learnable parameters.

Significant tracking performance improvements: The proposed feature transformation achieves remarkable performance gains on datasets featuring targets with visually similar appearance (e.g., DanceTrack and SportsMOT), boosting HOTA and AssA significantly across both appearance-only baselines and hybrid tracking frameworks (such as OC-SORT and Hybrid-SORT).

Broad generalization and thorough empirical analysis: The authors demonstrate applicability across diverse feature extractors (FastReID, MASA across various vision backbones) and multiple datasets (DanceTrack, SportsMOT, MOT17, MOT20, and TAO), supported by well-designed ablation experiments (e.g., comparing FLD against PCA and global supervised FLD).
weaknesses: Computational overhead and runtime scalability: Solving generalized eigenvalue problems online at each frame using CPU-based routines (e.g., scipy.linalg.eigh) cuts tracker throughput roughly in half (from 46.5 to 22.7 FPS, excluding detector runtime). Scaling to scenarios with high track counts and high-dimensional features (e.g., d=2048) poses practical efficiency challenges.

Limited gains on diverse-appearance scenarios: On benchmarks where targets already exhibit distinct visual appearance or where motion cues dominate (e.g., MOT17 and TAO), the improvement is marginal (e.g., +0.1 to +0.2 HOTA on OC-SORT-ReID on MOT17; +0.6 to +0.7 TETA on TAO), indicating the technique is primarily beneficial in visually ambiguous, uniform-appearance tracking domains.

Numerical stability details under-specified: In online tracking, the number of historical samples N within window T is typically much smaller than the raw feature dimensionality d (e.g., d=2048), making the within-class scatter matrix S_W rank-deficient/singular. The paper should clearly specify how singularity or matrix regularization is handled when computing the generalized eigenvectors.

strengths: Insightful and clearly articulated motivation: distinguishing targets in MOT is fundamentally a sequence-specific, closed-set discrimination task rather than an open-set retrieval problem. Utilizing tracking history to dynamically adapt feature representations addresses this discrepancy effectively.

Conceptually simple, training-free, and mathematically principled: adapting Fisher Linear Discriminant (FLD) using online tracklet histories as dynamic supervision provides closed-form subspace projections without requiring offline retraining.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple diverse benchmarks (DanceTrack, SportsMOT, TAO, MOT17, and MOT20) and various tracker paradigms (pure ReID trackers, hybrid trackers such as ByteTrack and OC-SORT, and foundation models via MASA).

Substantial empirical gains: the method achieves significant boosts in Association Accuracy (AssA) and overall HOTA, particularly in challenging scenarios with uniform appearance and complex motion (e.g., setting state-of-the-art results on SportsMOT with a pure ReID setup).

Detailed ablation studies and analytical verification, including the correlation analysis with the margin metric $\delta_{1000}$, the comparison between sequence-level history-aware FLD and dataset-level supervised FLD, and the effect of temporal weighting.
weaknesses: Potential numerical stability and singularity issues with FLD: the original feature dimension $d$ can be quite large (e.g., 2048 for FastReID), whereas the number of historical samples $N$ in early video frames or short windows $T$ can be smaller than $d$, causing the within-class scatter matrix $S_W$ to become singular. The manuscript does not detail whether regularization, shrinkage, or pseudo-inversion is applied to handle the ill-conditioned $S_W$.

Inference latency overhead: solving the generalized eigenvalue problem online causes an approximate 50% drop in frame rate (from 46.5 FPS to 22.7 FPS, excluding detector runtime), as it currently relies on CPU execution (`scipy.linalg.eigh`). Further discussion on updating frequency (e.g., solving FLD every $K$ frames) or GPU-friendly solver formulations would strengthen practical applicability.

Risk of error propagation: when early tracking errors or identity switches occur, the pseudo-supervisory track assignments will introduce label noise into the scatter matrices. While the temporal window and knowledge integration alleviate this to an extent, a quantitative analysis on tracking performance under high initial detection noise / false associations is lacking.

Marginal improvements on motion-dominated and appearance-diverse benchmarks such as MOT17 and TAO, indicating the technique primarily benefits scenarios characterized by visual homogeneity and complex non-linear motions.
